catalog_quote: "The vast majority of Lahu syllables receive sufficient stress so that their tonal contours do not significantly change regardless of the syntactic position of the syllable in the sentence. Completely stressless, and therefore toneless, syllables are excessively rare. The only examples are to be found in the speech of some fastidious speakers in a few recent loanwords from Burmese, Shan, or Thai.... A few native functor-morphemes do have reduced stress, however, to the point where their tones are affected. The negative adverbs 'm.a, high-falling' 'not' and 't-aspirated.a.high-falling' 'do not' are often treated this way in rapid speech, so that their tones are truncated and lose the final drop in pitch. This stress reduction is sometimes even marginally contrastive.... The only other syllable which typically has reduced stress is the noun-prefix /o-open/ with low-falling tone." (p. 34-35) [...] 490 $a TONE $A domain of tone: syllable $A "Every stressed syllable has a tone. Standard Lahu has five open (non-checked) tones, and two checked tones." (p. 21)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lahu is a seven-tone, strictly monosyllabic (omnisyllabic) language: every syllable is a stressed, tone-bearing unit, and the tone is not altered by position in the word or sentence. There is no rule placing a single word stress on one syllable of a polysyllabic word; polysyllables are compounds of full syllables. Stress is only ever reduced (with tonal truncation) on a handful of function morphemes: the negative adverbs mâ and thâ, the noun prefix ɔ̀-, and (per Matisoff) rare recent Burmese/Shan/Thai loans in careful speech; Bradley 1979: 119 adds that in Banian (Yellow Lahu) the prefix a-, the negatives ma, ta and the numerals te, ni take their pitch from the following syllable, and that Black Lahu negative adverbs 'are often not stressed'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened (no degrees of stress beyond full vs reduced).
new_statements.exceptions: Reduced stress (tone truncated, loses final pitch drop) on the negative adverbs mâ 'not' and thâ 'do not' in rapid speech — 'sometimes even marginally contrastive in the case of mâ, since there exists a homophonous..' [snippet cut] — and on the noun-prefix ɔ̀-; completely stressless/toneless syllables only in some fastidious speakers' recent loanwords from Burmese, Shan or Thai (e.g. 'coconut' mà?-paw for most speakers). Matisoff closes: 'A more detailed study of Lahu stress must await further research into Lahu intonation.'
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable/morpheme level within the sentence (Matisoff explicitly says tonal contour is stable 'regardless of the syntactic position of the syllable in the sentence'); citation forms and compounds are not separately discussed. Matisoff 2001 (snippet) adds that a string of verb particles 'as a whole has stress', i.e. some phrase-level grouping. Variety: 'standard' Black Lahu (Lahu Na) as spoken in northern Thailand.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement (Matisoff 1973) describes 'standard' Black Lahu (Lahu Na, Lahu-nâ?) as spoken by Matisoff's informants in northern Thailand; Matisoff 1988 treats Red Lahu and Lahu Shehleh as sub-dialects of Black Lahu, which is the dominant Lahu group in China and Burma, so it stands for lahu1253 [lhu]. Yellow Lahu / Lahu Shi (ISO 639-3 kds; Bradley's 'Banian', Paulsen 1996) is a separate, divergent languoid; Bradley 1979: 119 covers both, saying Black Lahu 'and most other dialects' leave the negative adverbs unstressed while Banian shows pitch assimilation of prefix/negative/numeral syllables.

tone_statements.quote: Lahu has seven tones, among which two tones are associated with tense vowels, and the other five tones are associated with lax vowels (see the Table 1). Matisoff (1982) transcribed the syllables of Tone 5 and Tone 6 as having a glottal stop coda. ... Table 1. The seven tones of Lahu. Lax Tone value Words ... Tone 1 33 ma33 woman Tone 2 21 ma21 classifier Tone 3 54 ma54 many Tone 4 45 ma45son-in-law Tone 7 11/112 ma11 teach ... Tense Tone value Words ... Tone 5 21 maʔ 21 army Tone 6 54 maʔ54 dream

tone_statements.summary: Seven tones given with Chao values (33, 21, 54, 45, 11/112 lax; 21, 54 tense/checked with creaky voice); F0 of tense tones 5/6 measured as near-identical to lax 2/3, contrast carried by duration and phonation. Nothing on TBU, sandhi or word stress.

tone_statements.citation: Jangjamras, Jirapat & Ratree Wayland. 2022. Tone Sandhi in Lahu Nyi. Journal of Liberal Arts, Prince of Songkla University 14(2): 141-180.
tone_statements.quote: Based on pitch contour analysis (Jangjamras et al., 2019), the Lahu Nyi seven-tone system has two glottalized tones and five non-glottalized tones, level and contour, as shown in Figure 1 ... Glottalized tones (Tones 3 and 6) occur in short syllables ending with a glottal stop. These two glottalized tones are shorter than the five non-glottalized tones. Tones 1 and 7 are level while tones 2, 4 and 5 are contour tones. Lahu Nyi does not have a vowel length distinction. In addition, tones 5 and 7 are slightly breathy at the end (Jangjamras et al., 2019).
tone_statements.locator: pp. 145 and 147, Literature Review, 1. Lahu Nyi Tone Description; Table 1 'Lahu Nyi Tone Description' on pp. 146-147 gives the Chao values 33, 41, 44ʔ, 45, 21, 21ʔ, 22
tone_statements.summary: Seven tones in Lahu Nyi (Red Lahu): 33, 41, 44ʔ (short, glottalized), 45, 21 (breathy), 21ʔ (short, glottalized), 22 (breathy); Table 1 adapted from the first author's 2019 acoustic study. Sandhi: mid>high (compounds), mid>high-rising (colours), high>low (causatives). No stress remark, pp. 141-150.

tone_statements.quote: It can be defined that the tonal system in Lahu Nyi language is phonemically distinctive features. And in the final conclusin, there are seven contrastive tonemes in Lahu Nyi language spoken in Chayi village. They are phonetically realized as level and rising tone, none of falling. ... Tone 1 22 = a mid low level tone / Tone 2 22? = a mid low level glottalized tone / Tone 3 33 = a mid level tone / Tone 4 44? = a mid high level tone / Tone 5 45? = a high contour glottalized tone / Tone 6 44 = a mid high level glottalized tone / Tone 7 45? = a high contour tone
tone_statements.locator: p. 81 (end of sec. 5.5.1) and p. 83 (sec. 5.5.3 Tonal Description)
tone_statements.summary: Seven tonemes on every syllable (Chao figures): five level (22, 33, 44; glottalized 22?, 44), two rising 45 (one glottalized); none falling; three glottalized. Typed figures for tones 4/6/7 misplace the glottal mark. Stress predictable, final syllable strong; vowel length conditioned by tone.

sources.citation: Bradley, David. 1979. Lahu dialects. Oriental Monograph Series 23. Canberra: Faculty of Asian Studies, Australian National University. 239 pp.
sources.note: Dialect survey with full phonologies. Only stress statement, p. 119 (Banian = Yellow Lahu section): in Banian the noun prefix a-, negative adverbs ma, ta, numerals te 'one', ni 'two' and some other first syllables of polysyllabic words take their pitch from the following syllable's tone; 'The negative adverbs in Black Lahu and most other dialects are Tone 1 syllables, with the appropriate pitch and contour features, but they are often not stressed.' No general stress rule; Black Lahu phonology (pp. 74-80) treats tone sandhi of the ɔ̀- prefix without mentioning stress.

sources.note: EGG + acoustic study showing a distinct tense-lax phonation contrast in Yunshan Lahu (multiple phonation types, tense-vowel front/back differences, length); historically tenseness comes from lost stop codas and relates to voiced/aspirated initials; 'in the process of transforming tense-lax features to tones, tense vowels retained their features of tenseness as a result of falling tones' - i.e. treats the checked/tense categories' relation to the tone system.
